title: Phase-controlled bipartite and tripartite entanglement and Bell nonlocality in a closed-loop optomechanical system
authors: Sha-Sha Zheng, Zi-Nan Wu, Di-Di Xu, Chang-Yu Li, Peng-Wei Gong, Qiongyi He, Feng-Xiao Sun
abstract: We propose a novel scheme to generate and manipulate bipartite and tripartite entanglement and Bell nonlocality in a closed-loop three-mode optomechanical system, where two optical modes are simultaneously coupled to a mechanical mode via typical optomechanical interactions and also coupled to each other through field transmission. This configuration gives rise to a phase-sensitive coupling, in which the relative phase directly controls the population distribution between two optical modes, enabling coherent redistribution of quantum correlations. By tuning this relative phase, we achieve deterministic switching of bipartite entanglement between two optical-mechanical pairs, as well as tunable genuine tripartite entanglement among three modes. Employing the displaced-parity measurement, we construct both the bipartite and tripartite Bell inequalities in phase space and observe maximal violations of approximately $2.32$ and $3$, respectively, which coincide exactly with the values achievable for ideal bipartite and tripartite Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen states. Counterintuitively, we find that the tripartite Bell nonlocality can persist even when the genuine tripartite entanglement is absent, providing deeper insight into the relationship between these two types of quantum correlations. Furthermore, we systematically analyze the effects of mechanical dissipation and thermal noise, identifying the parameter regions where Bell violation survives under realistic experimental conditions. Our results establish a comprehensive framework for generating, controlling, and verifying multipartite quantum correlations, paving the way towards phase-tunable quantum networks and noise-resilient tests of quantum foundations.
summary: This paper proposes a novel scheme to control entanglement and Bell nonlocality in a three-mode optomechanical system by tuning the relative phase between optical modes. The authors demonstrate maximal violations of Bell inequalities and reveal that tripartite nonlocality can exist independently of genuine tripartite entanglement. This establishes a framework for phase-tunable quantum networks and noise-resilient quantum tests.
main_problem: The paper aims to generate and manipulate bipartite and tripartite entanglement and Bell nonlocality within a closed-loop optomechanical system, while also clarifying the relationship between these quantum correlations.
main_result: The system allows for deterministic switching of bipartite entanglement and tunable genuine tripartite entanglement via phase control. Crucially, it demonstrates that tripartite Bell nonlocality can persist even when genuine tripartite entanglement is absent.
method: The analysis involves deriving quantum Langevin equations, constructing the covariance matrix for quadrature components, and using displaced-parity measurements to test Bell inequalities.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a closed-loop three-mode optomechanical system coupling two optical modes to one mechanical mode. The system dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian incorporating coupling terms and dissipation.
key_observables: Bipartite and genuine tripartite entanglement, bipartite and tripartite Bell nonlocality, and the relative phase ($\delta\varphi_0$) controlling correlations.
important_parameters: Relative phase ($\delta\varphi_0$), mechanical dissipation, and thermal noise levels.
main_assumptions: The analysis utilizes the quantum Langevin approach, and later sections rely on the adiabatic approximation and assumptions about the thermal state of mechanical noise.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the closed-loop three-mode cavity optomechanical setup. Other figures compare the maximized tripartite Bell function against the bipartite subsystem's Bell function.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the Hamiltonian and derivation of quantum Langevin equations, discusses the methods for constructing the covariance matrix, simulates phase control and noise effects, and concludes with a summary of the findings.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally relevant platform (optomechanics) to study fundamental quantum information concepts like multipartite entanglement and Bell nonlocality, offering insights into noise resilience and correlation structure.
